questions.explanation: The requirement for key material is unpredictability in both directions, and it is a requirement about the state rather than about the output. A general-purpose generator holds its whole history in a small structured state, advances it by a fixed rule, and produces a fixed number of bytes per call. Anyone who can observe a modest number of consecutive outputs can therefore run that rule backwards, recover the state, and regenerate every value the generator has ever produced, which is a different and much worse property than the values looking scattered. That is what makes the key recoverable from the generator's own behaviour rather than by search, and it is why key material has to come from a source designed for the job with a stated security claim rather than from one designed to be fast and pleasant. The second option is the most common belief and it confuses two different things: a distribution can look perfectly even and still be produced by a state an attacker can walk backwards through, and the length of the key protects against guessing the key, not against recovering it from the generator that made it. The third is the version of the worry that is only half right, since a clock seed makes the first value predictable and says nothing at all about the ones after it, which is why relying on the first one being the weak one is a very comfortable place to be wrong. The fourth is a real property of real code but a different property, and confusing the two is how a team ends up fixing the cache behaviour and leaving the state recoverable.

questions.explanation: Counter mode derives the keystream by encrypting the counter, so the counter is the only thing standing between one message and the same keystream as another. Once two messages under one key have used the same counter, the keystream is common to both and cancels when the two ciphertexts are exclusive-ored, leaving the exclusive-or of the two plaintexts. That is not a partial disclosure: with one of the plaintexts known or guessed, the other follows exactly, and even without it, a shared prefix shows up as zeros in the result and tells an attacker that the prefix is shared. The reason a restart is the dangerous event is that a counter that lives in memory is lost at exactly the moment it is most needed, and the natural repair, reseeding from something fresh, is precisely what reintroduces a value that has already been used. The second option is the belief that the secrecy of the key is the whole of the security, and it is a reasonable one to arrive at from the block-cipher case, where a nonce that repeats does leak the equality of plaintexts but little else; in counter mode the repeated value hands over the keystream. The third is the version that is true of a mode where the nonce is a chain that never goes backwards and false here, because a reset is a return to a value already used. The fourth describes a real but separate consequence that also happens in a mode where no keystream is recovered, and mistaking it for the mechanism leads teams to look for repeated ciphertexts rather than for a counter that starts again.

questions.explanation: The two values do different jobs and are held to different requirements, which is the whole reason the distinction is worth making. The key is the secret. Its secrecy is what the construction has to protect, its unpredictability is what stops an attacker from computing with it, and its length is a direct statement of how much work a search costs. The vector is not a secret at all. It is an input that makes the deterministic part of the cipher produce a different result each time, so that encrypting the same plaintext twice under the same key does not produce the same ciphertext twice and so that the first block of a chained mode has something to chain from. questions.explanation: A salt is public by design and is stored next to the value it produced, so the entire benefit has to come from what makes it per record rather than from hiding it. What per-record uniqueness buys is the defeat of shared work. An attacker who has taken a database gets one row, sees the salt and the setting, and can then spend their compute once over a large set of precomputed candidates rather than separately per account. If every row carries a different salt, that table has to be built separately for each one, and the cost of attacking a thousand accounts becomes a thousand times the cost of attacking one, which is the multiplication that makes a modest work factor worth choosing. It also means two people whose typed passwords are identical cannot be spotted from the stored values alone, which is a smaller benefit but a real one. The third is the version that survives in a surprising number of codebases, and the reason it is wrong is not speed but work reuse, since one salt means one table for everybody. The fourth confuses the salt with the derived key, whose length is a separate parameter entirely.

questions.explanation: Plain encryption gives you confidentiality and nothing else, which means it will happily decrypt a ciphertext that somebody has edited, and what comes out is a plaintext that is related to the original in a way the encrypting side never intended. In a chained mode the relationship is often something as crude as a chosen set of bit flips landing in chosen positions, and in a stream mode a single flipped bit flips the single corresponding plaintext bit. Integrity is the missing half, and the authenticated mode supplies it inside the construction rather than bolting it on: the tag is computed over the ciphertext and the nonce, it is checked before the plaintext is released, and a mismatch is the only answer the caller ever sees. The practical value is that it removes a category of mistake. Getting the ordering, the coverage and the failure behaviour right by hand is easy to get subtly wrong, and each way of getting it wrong is a real vulnerability, so a construction where the library holds the whole arrangement is worth a great deal even though its confidentiality is the same as an unauthenticated mode's. The second option describes a property no construction has, since holding the key has always been enough to decrypt and a tag changes nothing about that. The third is a serious and common misreading: the tag detects tampering, it does not repair it, and a repeated nonce leaks the same relationship it would have leaked without any authentication at all. The fourth is a separate feature that authenticated modes deliberately do not provide, because the tag is a fixed size and the ciphertext still has the length of the message.

questions.explanation: A message authentication code is a keyed integrity check, and the word doing the work in that sentence is keyed. Without a key, a digest can be recomputed by anyone who has the message, so a digest stored beside a message proves nothing against an attacker who can change both. With a key, only the holders of that key can produce the value, so producing one that verifies is something an attacker without the key cannot do. What that gives is the ability to detect modification and to detect a fabricated message, which is the property the name promises. What it does not give is any change to the message itself: the code travels beside the message, the message is still there in the clear, and anyone who can read the code can read the content. The second option is the most widespread belief and it is what a student writes down after meeting a keyed value for the first time, but it reverses the relationship, because the value is derived from the message rather than standing in for it. The third is the classic confusion between authentication and non-repudiation, and the reason it fails is visible in the construction itself: everyone who can verify can also produce, so a shared key gives both sides the ability to forge, and a signature scheme exists precisely because a verification key has to be public while a signing key does not. The fourth is the version of the third that is easy to miss when several services hold one key, and it is the reason a key shared across a trust boundary buys much less than it appears to.

questions.explanation: The property at stake is what a party who holds no key can learn and change by manipulating the bytes they can see. If the tag covers the ciphertext, then altering anything in the ciphertext invalidates a tag the attacker cannot recompute, so the recipient rejects the message before the decryption step produces anything at all, and the decryption itself never becomes an oracle. If instead the tag covers the plaintext and is then encrypted alongside it, the attacker cannot read the tag and cannot forge it, but the mode may still be malleable enough that a change to the ciphertext produces a corresponding change to the plaintext, and now there is a valid-looking pair whose tag is hidden rather than protected. The two orders are not equally good, and the good one is good for a structural reason rather than for any local cleverness: it fails safe at the first check instead of after decryption. The second option describes a real operational concern that both arrangements handle, because in either case the plaintext is not released until the tag has verified, so the ordering is not what stops a recipient acting on a forged message. The third is a genuine requirement, since a nonce that is not covered can be substituted, but both orderings can cover it and the difference between them is elsewhere. The fourth is a cost argument that does not discriminate at all, since a fixed-size tag costs the same to authenticate in either arrangement and the real overhead in the second is not performance but the loss of the early check.

questions.explanation: Length is one of the things encryption has never really hidden, and the interesting question is which constructions leak it and which pay to conceal it. A mode that encrypts by combining a keystream with the message, or by transforming each block independently, produces output whose length is a known function of the input length, and so the size of the record is a direct statement about the size of the message. A mode that pads, or that wraps the message in an explicit length field before encrypting, breaks that relationship so that all records of a class share a size. Neither is automatically wrong; the leak matters when the size of a message is itself the sensitive fact, which is common in fields where the length narrows the possibilities as sharply as the content, and it is a good reason to prefer a construction that conceals it. questions.explanation: A block size is a granularity, and almost every practical question about it follows from that word. The cipher is a function from one block of input to one block of output, so the block size fixes the unit over which the transformation is applied, and everything else is arranged around it: a message longer than one block has to be brought up to a multiple of the block size by padding or by an explicit length, and a message shorter than one block is padded out to a whole block, which is why a short message still produces a full block of output. It is emphatically not a strength parameter: strength comes from the round function and from the schedule, and a cipher with a larger block is not thereby harder to attack, it simply processes more at a time. The third confuses the data path with the key schedule, which produces round keys on a different schedule entirely. questions.explanation: A key schedule is a diffusion mechanism, and its job is to ensure that the family of keys is not a family with structure. If two keys that differ in one bit produced two sets of round keys that differ in one bit, then an attacker who found a weakness that works against keys differing in one bit would find it against every key, and the analysis would not have to be repeated per key. The schedule exists to break exactly that correspondence, so that neighbouring keys lead to unrelated round keys and an observation made on one key tells an attacker nothing useful about another. It is also where the key's own length is converted into the material the rounds consume, and a schedule that is cheap in time relative to the data path is a design goal rather than an accident, since encryption processes a great deal more data than keys and the expansion should not become the bottleneck. The second option has the logic the wrong way round: security never depends on hiding intermediate values, since every round key is used inside the cipher and any party who can observe the rounds can compute them, and designs assume exactly that observability. The third is a category error, because a schedule is not a key-wrapping scheme and nothing in ordinary rotation requires reversing it. The fourth inverts the purpose, since a slow schedule penalises the defender on every message while doing nothing to a search an attacker performs across many keys.
questions.hint: Ask what would be true of the round keys if two keys differed in a single bit.

questions.explanation: A key exchange solves one problem very well and leaves a second one completely untouched. What it solves is agreement on a secret that an eavesdropper cannot compute from the traffic, achieved without sending the secret itself in either direction. What it cannot do by itself is tell either party who it is talking to, and that is not a small gap, because the two situations are indistinguishable from the point of view of each honest party. In a direct exchange a middle party runs two of them, one with each side, and the two honest parties each derive the secret they expect and each send their traffic to the middle party, who forwards it, and everything looks fine to both. The middle party now holds both secrets, which is the entire problem. A certificate, a pre-shared key or a signature over the exchange parameters closes this by supplying the identity that the mathematics does not, and which of those is used is a deployment decision with real consequences. The second option confuses two independent properties: the strength of the derived value follows from the parameters and the participants' randomness, and authentication contributes nothing to it, which is why an unauthenticated exchange can produce a perfectly strong secret. The third is a specific and important property of a well-designed exchange, and the fact that it holds is exactly what makes the authentication problem the remaining one. The fourth mislocates the gap: both sides do complete and do agree on a value, and what they lack is evidence about the other side's identity.
questions.hint: Ask what an active party can do while sitting between two honest parties, and what each of them sees.

questions.explanation: Pinning works by making the client's expectation narrower than what the trust system would decide on its own, and every operational cost follows from that narrowing. The client no longer asks whether some authority vouches for this key; it asks whether this is one of the keys it was given. That is a real gain against an authority that has been coerced or misissued, and it is also a commitment: the set of acceptable keys is now fixed at the moment the client was built or configured, so the only way to change it is to get a new version of that list to the client. A rotation therefore has to be a two-step operation in which both the old and the new value are acceptable for a period, and the period has to be long enough that the new list has reached every installed client before the old key is retired. Skipping the overlap is the characteristic failure, and it is severe, because a client that has updated and a client that has not now disagree about which key is correct, and the ones that have not are broken in a way that no amount of server-side work can fix. The second option describes a different mechanism entirely, in which the client's expectation is refreshed continuously and the pin is really a preference; that is worth less than pinning and behaves nothing like it. The third overstates the effect, since a pinned client can still be told to stop trusting its pin, and the fourth confuses pinning a key with pinning an issuer, which are different things with different rotation costs.
questions.hint: Ask when the client's list of acceptable values can change, and what happens to the clients that missed the update.

questions.explanation: A certificate carries two distinct claims and it is worth separating them, because a self-signed one establishes the first and not the second. The first is a binding: this name is bound to this public key, and whoever holds the matching private key can speak for this name. The second is a judgement: this party is a suitable one for me to talk to, and it is normally reached by checking that some authority I already trust has said so. A self-signed certificate makes the binding without the judgement, because the signer is the same party as the subject, so the signature proves only that the holder of the key agrees with itself. That is enough when the two parties already have some other reason to believe each other, which is the normal reason it appears: a controlled fleet where the trust comes from the provisioning process, or a short-lived deployment where the trust is injected by the installer. The second option is the inference that produces a very common and very bad outcome, since an integrity check on a certificate is not a reputation judgement and a service with a perfect self-signature can be a hostile one. The third confuses the two claims in the other direction, and it is worth being concrete about why: a browser warns precisely because no accepted authority vouches for the name, and having the right name in the certificate is what makes the warning say which site is involved rather than being avoided. The fourth is simply false, since nothing about the signature constrains the validity dates, which is the same reason a self-signed certificate can be issued for twenty years.
questions.hint: Ask what a signature proves about who agreed to what, and whether the signer is anyone other than the subject.

questions.explanation: Revocation has an awkward property that nothing else in the trust system has: the document that carries the permission is not the document that carries the withdrawal, so the withdrawal has to reach the client separately and the client has to ask for it. That request is the source of everything awkward about revocation. It is a network operation on the critical path, it can be slow, it can fail, and the answer is only meaningful for a window of time, since a cached answer from last week says what was true last week. A client therefore needs three things and most real problems are one of the three being absent: a way to ask, a signature on the answer so it cannot be forged, and a freshness rule saying how long that answer is worth and what to do when no answer arrives at all. The second option is the belief that comes from thinking about files rather than trust decisions, and it is wrong for a structural reason: the key pair is what a certificate is built from, and the private half is needed to sign anything, so no third party can alter an issued certificate to mark it. The third is a reasonable mental model of a broadcast system and it does not describe what happens, because the authority cannot enumerate its clients and does not know where they are. The fourth is one real and common design, and it is genuinely how revocation scales in some deployments, but it is a design rather than the mechanism, and the distinguishing feature is the freshness rule rather than the list itself.
questions.hint: Ask where the withdrawal is written down, and what the client does when it cannot get an answer.

questions.explanation: The change is a substitution of mechanisms and it is a good one, but it only works if the replacement is actually in place. The cost of a conventional certificate is not the certificate; it is that withdrawing a key that turns out to be compromised requires a process, and that process is slow, global, and dependent on clients cooperating. Replacing the certificate every day makes that withdrawal unnecessary, because the key stops being usable on its own within a day without anyone having to act. The price is that a day has to be replaced by something, and it is replaced by automation: something must request the new certificate, store the private key where the service can use it and nothing else can read it, and put the new certificate where the service will actually pick it up. A human renewing a certificate daily is not a process, it is a queue, and a queue that runs once a day is a queue that will be late on the day it matters. The second option is the arithmetic of the idea taken too far: expiry does remove the need for an emergency withdrawal, but it replaces it with a routine renewal that is needed for the service to function at all, which is a harder requirement rather than a softer one. The third is a confusion of lifetime with custody, and the two are independent: a key that lives for a day and sits in a readable file is readable for a day, and one readable day is often the entire incident. The fourth is a real operational irritation that has nothing to do with the security argument, since chains are cached and re-fetched independently of the leaf.

questions.explanation: The value of this arrangement is entirely in where the key is not. In an ordinary deployment the key exists as a string in a configuration file, in an environment variable, in a heap, in a crash dump, in a backup and in whatever the process reads next; every one of those is a place an attacker who reaches the host can look, and each is a place where authorisation has already been won by the time anyone notices. A device that generates the key internally and performs operations with it internally removes the key from that list. What crosses the boundary is a request and a result, so the attacker who reaches the host can ask the device to do things, which is a much better position than being able to read the key and so being able to do anything, forever and offline. This is why the boundary is described as being around the key rather than around the data, and it is also why the design of the surrounding interface matters: a device that will decrypt for any caller inside the host has moved the problem rather than solved it, so authorisation of operations, use of distinct keys per purpose, and a policy about which operations are permitted without further approval are all part of the same job. The second option is the most common misreading and it is worth separating clearly, because the device does not touch the application data at all. The third and fourth are both things a device can help with, and a well-configured one does, but they are additions to the boundary rather than the boundary itself.

questions.explanation: The arrangement replaces one large trust with a collection of smaller ones, and the honest description of what it trusts is the whole set. The property it does buy is real: no single holder, and no group smaller than the threshold, can recover the key, so compromising one organisation is not enough, and a single dishonest custodian is not sufficient on their own. The property it does not buy is any protection against a sufficient group acting together, and a threshold scheme says nothing about the willingness of the holders to cooperate when asked by someone with a legal right to ask. It also introduces a new party into the trust picture, which is the threshold itself: who decides the number, who can change it later, and who administers the recombination. That party becomes as significant as any holder, and in a design where the administration is run by the same organisation that asked for the escrow, the reduction in trust is smaller than it looks. The second option describes an ordinary single-custodian escrow with extra steps, and it is the belief the arrangement is usually adopted to avoid. The third confuses the guarantee with the mechanism, since recombination being required is what makes the split work and says nothing about anybody's behaviour. The fourth is a genuine and valuable property, namely that one compromise is insufficient, but it is a side effect of the threshold rather than a separate guarantee, and it evaporates the moment the threshold holders are approached together.

questions.explanation: The cost of a collision is not the cost of the digest space but its square root, and the reason is that an attacker can build a large set of candidates, hash them all, and look for any two that agree, which finds a pair in roughly the square root of the number of possible outputs rather than the number itself. That is the birthday bound, and it is why a digest twice as long is considered dramatically harder to collide. The consequence is a substitution: two different inputs, one digest, and a system that verifies the digest and therefore accepts both. That matters wherever the digest is what a signature or a certificate attests to, since the whole point of signing a digest is to bind the signed claim to the bytes, and a collision breaks that binding. The second option describes the work to find an input matching a digest you already hold, which is the preimage problem and is a different and much harder one. The third is a common and total misreading: being able to compute a function forward says nothing about being able to invert it, and a hash is deliberately built so that the second does not follow. The fourth compares the two problems in a way that is exactly backwards, since the preimage search is the harder of the pair and a password search is a much smaller problem than either.
questions.hint: Ask how many candidates the attacker can hash and compare at once, rather than how many outputs exist.

questions.explanation: The difference is who pays, and the two constructions are designed for different threat models because of it. A password hash is stored in a row that the attacker may well hold, so the hash must assume the attacker will recompute it as fast as the hardware allows, and the entire design response is to make each of those recomputations expensive. That is why the cost setting is a first-class parameter and why it is stated in the stored row, so that a verification can find it and an attacker has to use the same one. A keyed digest is a different animal: it exists to let two parties who already share a key detect modification of a message, and its security rests on the key, not on the cost, so it is fast by design because it is applied to data in flight. The second option is a real confusion and it is worth being explicit that it is false: a function is deterministic or it is not, and the slowness comes from repeating a deterministic step, so a later verification produces the same value at a higher cost. The third mistakes a shared secret for protection against an offline attack, when the attacker who has the row has the message and can simply recompute. The fourth is the belief that produces the most damage in practice, since a team that reaches for a fast keyed function to store passwords has built something that offers no cost to an attacker at all.

Change any of those and the digest is unchanged, so the signature still verifies and the thing it was supposed to say about has moved. The correct fix is to define a canonical form that includes every field that carries meaning, with the field names bound as well as the values, and to sign that. The third is closer to the truth and is a useful practical reminder, since the canonical form is a design decision that has to be checked at each use, and two systems that sign different canonical forms are not interoperable. questions.explanation: A timestamp authority does one narrow thing, and the value of the whole mechanism is in how narrow it is. It receives a value, records the fact that this value existed at this time, and issues a signed statement about it, which means the statement can be relied on as something a third party could not have back-dated. What that buys is a floor under the age of the signature. Without one, a signature presented years later is ambiguous: it may have been made when it should have been, or it may have been made after a key was compromised, and there is no way to tell from the signature itself. With one, the ambiguity is gone, and a signature that predates a disclosure of key compromise is evidence that it was not made with knowledge of that compromise. The other three options each attribute a capability to the authority that it does not have. It does not check who the signer is; it is given a value and has no opinion about who produced it, which is why it is usable for a signature whose signer's status is contested. It does not hold or compare documents; it never sees them. And it does not validate keys, since key validity is the signer's business and is exactly the thing that may be in doubt when a timestamp matters.

questions.explanation: A revocation answer is a statement about a moment, and that is the whole reason the moment is part of the signed content. questions.explanation: The useful reframing is that homomorphic encryption moves a boundary rather than removing a risk. In an ordinary deployment the party that has to do the work also has to see the inputs, because the inputs arrive in the clear and the work happens where they can be read. A homomorphic construction moves the work to a party that cannot read the inputs: it receives ciphertexts, applies the function to them, and returns ciphertexts of the result, and the holder of the key decrypts at the end. The fourth reduces a deployment change to a mathematical identity, which is true and is why the result is correct, and it is not an argument that the change is unnecessary.

Raising it means fewer holders acting alone can recover the key, which is the confidentiality side and the reason to raise it: the compromise of one or two organisations no longer suffices. questions.explanation: What short lifetimes buy is a bound on exposure, and it is a bound on time rather than on anything else. A key that lives for a year is worth a year to whoever takes it, no matter how the leak happened. A key that lives for a day is worth a day, and the withdrawal happens on its own, which is why the expensive part of revocation disappears. What does not change is the past. Everything encrypted under the key while it was valid remains encrypted under that key, and whoever holds the key can still read all of it, so a service that has been running for a year under the long-lived key has a year of history that the change does nothing about, and a long-lived key that has already leaked has already exposed all of it. This is the practical reason to combine the change with an inventory and a rotation of the existing material rather than treating it as a forward-looking improvement. The second option introduces a claim about identity that is unrelated, since a credential's lifetime says nothing about who or what it is issued to. The third inverts the relationship between a key and the data, since a key protects every record under it rather than a window of them. The fourth is close and its omission is instructive: it lists the benefit and then quietly drops the requirement that made the benefit possible, and without that requirement the shorter lifetime only means the key is exposed more often.
questions.hint: Ask what the key is worth to whoever took it, and what the change does for what was already written.

questions.explanation: The routine makes three assertions and all three are about the certificate itself rather than about where it came from. The dates say the certificate claims to be current, the name says it claims to be about this host, and both are claims the certificate makes about itself, so accepting them is close to accepting the certificate's own account of itself. What is missing is the chain: the signature has to be checked against a key the client already trusts, and the chain of that key has to lead to a root in the client's trust store. Without that step, anyone can produce a certificate with any name, any dates, and a signature made with a key they generated a minute ago, and this routine will accept it. The second option describes a belief that is close to the truth and inverted in a consequential way, since the trust store is the entire basis of the decision and not a place revocation is looked up. The third claims a check that is not in the code, and the fact that the routine would not notice is the finding. The fourth is the reasoning that makes the finding survivable in a review, since a certificate that expires does stop being a problem, and a self-minted one is typically given a long life precisely so that it does not.

questions.explanation: Both arrangements do the same underlying job and the difference is the size of the set of parties the client is relying on. Under the ordinary arrangement the client trusts a root, that root vouches for the issuer, the issuer vouches for the name, and a compromise or a coercion anywhere along that chain is inherited silently. A pin removes the middle of the chain: the client accepts a key it was given and nobody else's judgement is involved. What does not change is the thing the client is actually proving, which is that the party presenting holds the private key matching a key it accepts for a name. The name binding, the signature check and the proof of key control are identical in both designs, and a client that skips them is unprotected in either. That is the point the options are drawing at, and it is the one that gets lost when pinning is described as making a connection safe. The second and third are each half right and both stop at the wrong place, and the omissions in them are the same omission: a pin on a host that is already compromised is a pin the attacker can read, and that host is the single most common way a connection is intercepted. The fourth is the argument that ends the discussion without examining it, since the trust system does not cover a coerced issuer and that is the case pinning exists for.
questions.hint: Ask how many parties the client is trusting in each case, and what both still have to prove.

questions.explanation: The two designs differ in where the binding to the bytes happens and both are legitimate, and the differences follow entirely from that. Signing the file puts the bytes inside the signature, so any change to them breaks the check, and nothing about the name, the version or the publisher is committed. Signing a record moves the file out of the signature and puts an identification of it inside, which means the record's own content is protected, so the name and the version cannot be altered, and the file is bound only as well as the identification binds it. That identification is the crux: a reference that is exact makes the two designs equivalent in strength for the file, and a reference that is loose, such as a name without a digest, means a different file with the same name is accepted. The second option is the belief that makes the choice seem arbitrary, and the convention is not free, it is a contract between the signer and everyone who verifies, and two parties with different conventions get different guarantees from the same word. The third is a false ranking that comes from treating the bytes as the only thing worth binding. The fourth adds work for no gain, since a consumer checking both is checking a property neither of them provides alone.
questions.hint: Ask where the file's bytes enter each signature, and what the second one binds instead.

options.misconception: requires both

Moving the key into a device removes it from that list, which is a large and genuine reduction in the number of ways it can leak. What it does not change is anything about the signature or the policy. The same bytes are committed, the same verification is required downstream, and the device will sign whatever the pipeline asks it to sign, so a compromise of the pipeline now has a signing capability without a key to take, which is better than before and is not the same as being safe. The authorisation question, who may ask this device to sign what, is where the remaining risk lives and it has to be answered separately. questions.explanation: Separation is about blast radius, and the honest way to state its effect is in terms of what a single compromise reaches. With one key, a compromise reaches every record, present and future, and there is no way to limit that without changing the key. With a key per purpose, a compromise of one purpose key reaches the records under that purpose and nothing else, and every other purpose continues to be protected by a key that is still secret. That is the whole benefit and it is worth having. It is not a complete one, and the reason is in the design: the derived value per record is derived from the purpose key, so an attacker holding that key can derive the value for any record under that purpose, including records written after the compromise, so the exposure grows for as long as the key is in use. Bounding that further needs rotation, which is why separation and rotation are complementary and why a design with per-purpose keys and no rotation has traded one problem for a smaller version of the same problem. The second denies the effect outright, which is the belief that makes the change look pointless. The third gets the rotation benefit right and the containment wrong, and it is the most common way the trade is misremembered. The fourth is the same confusion framed as a confidentiality gain.
questions.hint: Ask how many records one compromised key reaches, and whether it reaches records written afterwards.

options.text: It changes the cost of a rotation, since one purpose key rotates independently of the others, and it does not change how many records a single leak reaches, because the derived value is bound to the same purpose key

options.misconception: correct on the first, silent on the second
options.text: It changes the confidentiality of the data at rest, so records under one purpose are no longer readable with a key obtained for a different purpose, and it does not change the number of keys in use

questions.explanation: The change closes a specific hole for what is written after it, and it is worth being clear about the boundary because the boundary is where the residual risk lives. After the change, a record whose tag does not verify is refused before anything is decrypted, so the alteration that a mode without integrity permits no longer works on new records. Records already stored are untouched by the change: they were written without tags, they have no tag to check, and they are still exactly as alterable as they were. So the honest description of the state after the change is that the new scheme is protected and the old data is not, and closing that second gap means a migration in which records are re-sealed under a scheme that produces a tag, which is a deliberate and somewhat expensive operation rather than a configuration change. The second option describes that migration and presents it as a side effect of deploying, which would be a serious misunderstanding of the deployment. The third confuses the two properties, since a tag says nothing about who can read the plaintext and constrains nothing about which plaintexts can be produced. The fourth is wrong in a way that matters, because a server that requires a tag rejects the untagged clients, and the migration is a server-side change with the clients following.

questions.explanation: The technical situation is genuinely identical and the organisational one is not, and it is worth being clear about which is which because the difference drives every practical choice. The same facts, the same urgency and the same exposure apply whoever wrote the code, and a finder who discovers the supplier is the author gains no time. What differs is leverage. An organisation that owns the code can decide to fix it, choose the date, and describe the problem in public on its own schedule, so a private report can be followed by a disclosure the organisation controls. A supplier decides whether and when to ship, and the finder has no way to make it happen, which is why the supplier case is the one that needs a deadline and why the obligation to tell users rests with whoever distributes the product, which in that case is the supplier and not the finder. The second option is the reduction that produces surprise, because everything after the first contact is where the leverage difference lives. The third assumes the distributor is the same in both cases, which it is not. The fourth puts the entire difference in a contractual detail and calls the technical risk identical, which is true and irrelevant, since the question is not what is at stake but who will act.

questions.explanation: The inventory comes first because every later step is only as correct as the list of consumers, and the characteristic failure in a re-key is a reader that was not known to be a reader, which then breaks at the worst moment. Provisioning second is what makes the change reversible, since until new material is proven to work there is nothing to gain by committing. The re-seal is third because it is the step that has to be observed from the consumers' side: the store can report itself healthy while a reader that reads by a different path is going nowhere, and the only signal is that reader's own error rate. Retiring the old key is last deliberately, because it is the one step that is not reversible, and because retiring it too early is the failure that turns a planned migration into an outage for any consumer that was missed. Done in another order, either the store is committed before the material is proven or the old key disappears while a consumer is still reading through it. The confirmation in the last step is what distinguishes a migration that finished from one that appears to have finished.

Establishing use first is the step with a deadline, because the evidence of ongoing use is available now and decays quickly, and it is also the step that distinguishes a key that has been copied from one that has been copied and is being exercised, and those two situations have different urgencies. answer.exemplar: The honest reason is that the two-step arrangement is not wrong, it is a set of decisions that somebody has to make and that nobody reviews. What has to be decided: what the integrity value covers, whether the ciphertext or the plaintext is what gets signed, which of those two steps happens first, whether the check happens before any plaintext is produced or after, what happens when the integrity value does not match, and whether that failure is distinguishable from any other failure. Each of those is individually reasonable, each has a defensible wrong answer, and the questions are not visible at the call site because the API presents the same two calls either way. Two arrangements illustrate the range. If the check runs first over the ciphertext and the failure produces one answer for every cause, then a party with no key cannot alter a record and cannot learn anything by asking, and the implementation is sound. If the padding is examined before the check, then the failure distinguishes a body whose padding is wrong from one whose integrity value is wrong, and a caller who can tell those apart has a way of asking a question about a chosen block and getting a bit back, which is sufficient to recover plaintexts without holding the key. Neither arrangement is a mistake anybody would make on purpose, which is exactly the argument for a construction that removes the choice. An authenticated mode removes all six decisions at once: the tag covers the ciphertext and the nonce, it is checked before the plaintext is released, one comparison decides acceptance, and one answer covers every failure. The gain is not a stronger guarantee, since a correctly composed two-step arrangement gives the same one. The gain is that the guarantee survives being written by someone who has not thought about it, which is the normal condition under which software is written, and that is the only argument that scales.

questions.explanation: The two-step arrangement is not weaker when it is composed correctly; it is weaker in practice, because it leaves six decisions to the implementer and each has a defensible wrong answer. An authenticated mode removes all six at once, and the guarantee it gives is the same one a correct composition gives. The value is in the guarantee surviving contact with an implementer who has not thought about it.

answer.exemplar: Shortening the validity period changes one thing precisely: the length of time during which a key that has been taken is still accepted. That is a real and worthwhile bound, because most of the harm from a leaked long-lived key comes from the period in which nobody knows it has been taken, and a credential that stops being accepted on its own removes the need for a withdrawal process to be fast, global and reliable. It is worth being clear that this is a forward-looking property. A signature made under a key that has since been taken carries no marker of when it was made, so a verifier presented with it after the key expired has no basis for treating it differently from one made before, and the artefact remains usable until something else happens. Data encrypted under the key is the same in a stronger form: it is not merely that nobody can date it, it is that the person holding the key can read all of it, including everything written after the compromise, and shortening the lifetime does not change that for the records already written. Two consequences follow, and both are about work that a forward-looking change does not do. The first is that a key that was in use before the change needs its own treatment, and the honest options are to re-key the data, to accept the historical exposure explicitly, or to shorten the exposure by rotating and re-sealing, and the choice depends on what the data is worth. The second is that a timestamp attached at the time of signing is what lets a later verifier distinguish a signature made before a disclosure from one made after it, which is why an independent attestation of signing time is worth having independently of any short-lived credential. The general shape is the same as for a password: rotating a credential bounds what is stolen in future and does not retrieve what has already been used.

questions.explanation: A short validity bounds how long a taken key is still accepted, which removes the need for a fast withdrawal. It does not date what was already produced: a signature made under the key is not marked, and anything encrypted under it stays readable to whoever holds it. Re-keying the past and timestamping signatures are the two pieces of work the change does not do.

answer.exemplar: The two properties are about different questions and confusing them leads directly to the wrong answer about digest length. Preimage resistance asks whether anybody who holds a digest can find an input that produces it. Collision resistance asks whether anybody can find any two inputs that produce the same digest, without either of them being specified in advance. They are not the same difficulty and the reason is that a collision search can be organised as a single large effort: build a large set of candidate inputs, hash them all, and look for two that agree, which finds a pair after roughly the square root of the number of possible outputs. A preimage search has no such organisation available, because the target digest is fixed and every candidate has to be tested against it, so the work is proportional to the whole output space. A digest chosen to resist collisions must therefore be roughly twice as long as one chosen only to resist preimages, which is why the two numbers quoted for a function are different numbers and why a function that quotes only one of them is leaving out the claim that matters for a particular use. For signing a document, collision resistance is the property that matters, and the reason is worth spelling out. A signature commits to a digest, and a verifier checks that the digest of the document it was given equals the digest that was signed. If a second document exists with the same digest, a verifier will accept that second document against a signature made for the first, and nothing in the verification can detect it, because the digests are equal and that is the whole test. Neither property is a confidentiality property, and neither has anything to say about whether the digest can be inverted to recover the document, which is a third claim and generally the one a password storage design is actually relying on.

questions.explanation: Preimage resistance is harder than collision resistance, so a digest sized only for preimages is too short for signing. Signing needs collisions, because a verifier only compares digests, so a second document with the same digest is accepted against a signature made for the first.
questions.hint: Ask whether the target digest is fixed in advance, and what a verifier actually compares.

answer.exemplar: A signature answers exactly one question: this value was produced by the holder of the private key matching the key the verifier checked against. That is a real answer, and it is what makes a signature useful, because it cannot be produced by anyone else and it cannot be altered afterwards. What it does not answer is any question about permission. The key holder may be the right organisation and may be signing a statement it had no authority to issue; the key may belong to an individual who signed something only their manager could approve; the signature may predate the moment the individual was given the responsibility that the statement concerns. Nothing in the cryptography distinguishes these cases, because a signature has no opinion about what the signer's role is, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight: the verification key is public by design, so anybody can obtain it and check a signature, and a check that depended on a private fact about the signer's authority could not be performed by the people who most need to perform it. Authority therefore has to come from somewhere outside the signature, and there are two ordinary places for it. The first is the binding between the key and the role, which is what a certificate provides: a trusted party asserts that this key is this organisation's for this purpose, and the assertion is worth exactly what that party is worth. The second is the check on the statement itself, where the signature attests to a request and a separate decision by someone entitled to grant it is what makes the request effective. The general form is worth stating because it recurs outside cryptography: an artefact that proves origin does not prove authority, and any system that treats the two as the same has a gap exactly as wide as the difference between who made a thing and who was allowed to make it.

questions.explanation: A signature proves which key signed which bytes and nothing about permission. Authority has to come from a binding between the key and a role, such as a certificate, or from a separate decision by whoever is entitled to grant what was requested.

Computing it also makes the asymmetry concrete: the defender runs the function a handful of times a day for one user, while the attacker with a stolen table runs it once per candidate, so a threefold increase costs the defender an amount nobody notices and costs the attacker three times as much for every one of their guesses. The same calculation in the other direction is the one that goes wrong in practice, since a setting chosen to be generous for a fast machine can be marginal for a slow one, and the ratio between the two is a more stable figure than either absolute number. Two mistakes are worth naming. Treating the setting as a key length is the common one, and it produces systems that are long and fast, which is the opposite of the intent. And choosing the figure once and never revisiting it is the second, because the defender's hardware improves and the attacker's improves too, and the ratio between them is the only thing that has actually been held constant by the choice.

questions.explanation: The number is 16777216, which is two to the twenty-fourth and also 256 multiplied by 256 multiplied by 256, and it is worth doing both ways because the arithmetic is the whole point of the item. The figure is not enormous in the way a two-byte or four-byte choice might suggest to a reader, and the practical consequence is a rate rather than a number: a service writing a hundred records a second exhausts this counter in a little under forty-seven hours, which means any design that uses a three-byte counter and restarts its process on a schedule is in permanent nonce reuse, and the number of distinct values is not the thing that saves it. What saves it is either a counter wide enough that the whole life of the key fits inside it, which is why counters in serious designs are wide enough to be effectively never exhausted under a key, or a construction that tolerates the wrap, which is what the authenticated modes with a wider internal state are for. The two mistakes worth naming are treating the counter as a random value, which wastes the space and gives up the guarantee that comes from knowing the values do not repeat, and treating the count as safe because it is large, which is the reasoning that produces a design that works in testing and fails on the first busy afternoon. The figure to hold on to is not the number but the relationship between the counter's width, the write rate and the length of time one key is in use.
